title: Climate change and sovereign risk
summary: This ECB Financial Stability Review special feature examines how climate change affects sovereign balance sheets through physical risks (natural catastrophes) and transition risks (disorderly move to net-zero). It highlights contingent liabilities that may emerge from climate-related fiscal pressures, insurance gaps, and feedback loops between sovereign credit conditions and financial stability. The report notes that only a quarter of disaster losses are currently insured in the EU, creating potential fiscal vulnerabilities as extreme weather events intensify.
key_points: Physical and transition risks can directly impact public finances through adaptation costs, disaster recovery, and transition investments while indirectly affecting tax revenues as risks materialize in the real economy
Sovereigns face contingent liabilities through the financial sector (credit losses, explicit/implicit guarantees) and insurance coverage gaps that governments may be asked to cover
Feedback loops can amplify financial stability risks: rising contingent liabilities + sovereign debt sustainability concerns lead to deteriorating sovereign credit conditions and ratings
EU has reduced emissions by over 30% compared to 1990 levels but must reduce fossil fuel share from 65% (2022) to 50% by 2030 for current targets, or 31% to limit warming to 1.5°C
Only approximately 25% of disaster losses in the EU are currently insured, leaving significant fiscal exposure
Countries with high physical risk exposure and large insurance protection gaps face the greatest vulnerabilities from contingent liabilities materializing
why_it_matters: This analysis is relevant for sovereign debt investors, financial stability regulators, and policymakers assessing climate-related fiscal risks in the EU. As climate events intensify, countries with high physical risk and low insurance coverage may face sovereign credit deterioration and rating pressure, potentially creating feedback loops with the financial sector. The analysis supports the case for accelerated green capital market development and adaptation investment to mitigate these risks.
macro_context: The analysis frames climate change as a material macro risk factor for sovereign debt sustainability. EU climate targets require halving fossil fuel share by 2030. Physical risk exposure combined with low insurance penetration creates contingent fiscal liabilities that could affect sovereign borrowing costs and credit ratings. The report notes that fiscal support has historically mitigated climate-related financial stability risks, but vulnerabilities may increase as extreme events intensify.
